content.title: FOOD FACTS THAT SOUND MADE UP BUT ARE 100% REAL
facts: **Cashews** are never sold in their shell to consumers — the shell contains a resin closely related to poison ivy's, and it has to be steamed off before the nut is safe to touch.
**Nutmeg** contains a natural compound called myristicin that, in large doses, is genuinely hallucinogenic — the same class of effect found in some synthetic drugs.
**Carrots** were originally purple, not orange — the orange variety was bred by Dutch growers in the 1600s, likely as a tribute to the House of Orange.
**Strawberries** aren't technically berries, but bananas are — botanically, a true berry needs seeds inside its flesh, which bananas have and strawberries don't.
**Almonds** are actually seeds of a fruit closely related to peaches — the fuzzy green fruit around them is usually stripped away before you ever see it.
**Wasabi** sold in most restaurants outside Japan isn't real wasabi at all — it's typically dyed horseradish, because real wasabi root is expensive and spoils fast.
**Chewing gum** has been found in the stomachs of mummies from ancient Sweden dating back over 9,000 years, made from birch bark tar people chewed for its antiseptic taste.

content.caption:
A few of these deserve a second look. Cashews are one of the only common nuts you'll never see sold raw in the shell to regular shoppers — the resin between the shell and the nut is chemically similar to urushiol, the same irritant in poison ivy, so processors steam or roast it away industrially before it ever reaches a store. Nutmeg seems harmless sprinkled on your latte, but myristicin, one of its natural oils, is metabolized by the body into a compound structurally similar to certain amphetamines — which is exactly why more than a tablespoon or two can cause real, unpleasant hallucinogenic effects. And wasabi is the one that surprises people most: true wasabi root oxidizes and loses its flavor within about 15 minutes of being grated, so almost no restaurant outside Japan can keep up with fresh supply, which is why dyed horseradish paste became the global stand-in.
